Breaking: AI Told These Ex-Google Guys How to Build a Billion-Dollar Weapons Business

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1156 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, when Silicon Valley entrepreneur Chad Steelberg decided he wanted to get involved in the war in Ukraine, he had no idea where to start.
  • Steelberg, alongside fellow Google alumnus and former Apple executive Andy Baynes, states they are trying to break the Russia-Ukraine war “stalemate,” Silicon Valley–style.
  • In a recent development, steelberg, originally from Newport Beach, California, started itching to “make a difference” on the battlefield after he took in a couple hundred Ukrainian refugees into his French chateau in early 2022.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, when Silicon Valley entrepreneur Chad Steelberg decided he wanted to get involved in the war in Ukraine, he had no idea where to start. So the then CEO of enterprise AI organization Veritone did what he knew best: built an artificial intelligence model to help him figure it out. Today, he has proprietary munition and missile designs, several government partnerships, and a defense-as-a-service business valued at more than $1 billion.

Steelberg, alongside fellow Google alumnus and former Apple executive Andy Baynes, states they are trying to break the Russia-Ukraine war “stalemate,” Silicon Valley–style. They believe their experience building and iterating technology rapidly can help bring Western weapon manufacturing in line with the rapid innovation cycles seen on the battlefield and beat the “attritional cat-and-mouse technology game” that the war, as Baynes describes it, has become.

In a recent development, steelberg, originally from Newport Beach, California, started itching to “make a difference” on the battlefield after he took in a couple hundred Ukrainian refugees into his French chateau in early 2022. He says he was regularly “heartbroken” by the outpouring of grief whenever bad news arrived about a husband, father, or son back home. “I believe I could really change the outcome of this and every war,” Steelberg tells WIRED. "I'm not saying this is purely altruistic,” he adds. “Of course we're going to be making money doing it.".

This week, their firm, Tiberius Aerospace, stated it had secured $85 million in Series A financing, led by European technology investment firm Lakestar and Rochefort Asset Management, a national-security-focused investment firm licensed under the US Defense Department. Ukrainian venture capital firm UA1 is also an investor.

Tiberius began as Steelberg’s private research lab, incorporated in 2021, which employed people across France, the UK, and US to experiment on left-field ideas across a range of technologies, from drones and electric vertical takeoff aircraft to quantum computing. After the invasion, he pivoted the lab’s AI and aerospace engineers into writing code and building spreadsheets to objectively analyze the war’s many factors and calculate what could move the needle. The AI model they created swiftly ruled out building better defensive technology because that would just harden the stalemate.

With his aim narrowed to building an offensive weapon, Steelberg developed several metrics to numerically analyze the lethality of different systems, including cost-effectiveness, and used the AI engine to simulate weapons under different conditions and identify what would disrupt the market. Don’t build another drone, it suggested, build longer-range artillery munitions. The resulting system, called Sceptre, can be fired from a 155-millimeter howitzer—the most common artillery weapon donated to Ukraine. As well as traveling farther than currently available rounds, they claim they can reach supersonic speeds and altitudes beyond jamming range.

Giving Ukraine’s guns extra range is notable, Sam Cranny-Evans, an associate fellow at UK defense think tank the Royal United Services Institute, tells WIRED, because it would allow Ukrainian gunners to operate beyond the reach of Russian drone attacks. 155-mm shells “can cause massive damage to a group of vehicles or infantry,” he indicates. “Any technology that can help Ukraine extend the reach of its howitzers and return them to combat would be valuable.”.

With a prototype he’d designed with the help of AI, Steelberg also started to expand the Tiberius team, including bringing on board Baynes as chief strategy officer in 2023. Baynes had first traveled to Ukraine around a decade ago to investigate how local startup Ring, now owned by Amazon, had outdone Nest, which he’d been working on and eventually sold to Google. He fell in love with Kyiv’s ambitious software engineers and booming tech scene–responsible for globally successful tech tools like Grammarly and Snapchat’s face filters. In 2016, he bought a local life-science tech company with the aim of accelerating next-generation medicines through automating clinical trials and improving protein modeling. “What drew me into Kyiv was the hunger and ambition in the engineering community,” he tells WIRED. “It was difficult to not be enormously attracted to that and to see if it's something that could be put into really critical-mission problem sets like cancer drugs or speeding up clinical trials for life-science companies.”.

According to recent reports, after the Russian invasion, Baynes set himself up in Budapest for around six months to help with the logistics of evacuating women and children and moving equipment into the country. He asked his global network for help finding medical equipment, vehicles, and accommodation for refugees—bringing him back in touch with Steelberg. Baynes believes the West’s response to the invasion has been “inadequate” and that Ukraine needs better offensive capabilities to push Russia’s army back.

It has been revealed that in April, Tiberius announced it had successfully fired one of its Sceptre projectiles from a NATO-standard 155-mm howitzer for the first time. It is now working with the US Army to mature the system, and it has announced a $500 million technology collaboration contract with UK partners to manufacture, license, and distribute the munition. It is also developing a missile, which it expects to start generating revenue next year.

It has been revealed that tiberius has turned the AI system it initially built into a product called GRAIL (Generative Real-Time Artificial Intelligence for Lethality). Steelberg states he is “most excited about” this. He hopes the platform can enable continuous upgrades to the weapon designs Tiberius licenses by decentralizing manufacturing. Steelberg says that, as well as automating supply chain management and compliance, the software simulates weapons against different targets in a range of environments and weather conditions, such as an Arctic peninsula. In addition to open-sourced data, the team is trying to get hold of much sought-after active combat data from around the world, including Ukraine. The idea is that this all enables consumers to test, iterate, and design weapons for specific uses much quicker.

“In the world of AI and design and development getting faster and faster, what is it that the West or the group of allied nations have an undeniable advantage on?” Baynes asks. “If you can weaponize all of the spare capacity and precision manufacturing across the UK, France, Germany, the Nordic countries, the US,” he notes, “that's something that our adversaries today can never ever match.” Tiberius aims to achieve this by copying “the Apple model,” continues Baynes, who reported to Steve Jobs for four years. He says outsourcing manufacturing to many third-party subcontractors can accelerate development and deployment and keeps expensive production costs off Tiberius’ balance sheet during peacetime.

It has been revealed that “We're taking the approach of Silicon Valley,” notes Steelberg. “When you run into a big, hard, hairy problem, you not only cross that, but you turn around, you build a bridge—it’s a toll bridge, obviously—so the entire industry can cross that hurdle faster, better, stronger. They might pay a small fee, but it's better than dying in the ditch and not making it across it.”.

Klarna tops $1bn in revenue for a fourth quarter, still loses $65m

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (483 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Thenextweb

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Klarna grew revenue 12% to $1.009bn in the third quarter of 2026, its fourth quarter in a row above $1bn.
  • It still made a net loss of $65m, compared with a $95m loss in the same quarter of 2025.
  • “Q3 was our fourth straight quarter with revenue above 1 billion dollars and positive adjusted operating income.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Klarna grew revenue 12% to $1.009bn in the third quarter of 2026, its fourth quarter in a row above $1bn. Adjusted operating income reached $21m, up from a $14m loss a year ago, the Swedish payments company said on Tuesday.

It still made a net loss of $65m, compared with a $95m loss in the same quarter of 2025. The operating loss was $53m. Klarna put this down to share-based payments, which rose 38% to $54m in its annual pay cycle, according to its earnings release.

“Q3 was our fourth straight quarter with revenue above 1 billion dollars and positive adjusted operating income. We are keeping more of each dollar we process through our everyday finance network,” CEO Sebastian Siemiatkowski noted.

Recent findings suggest that shoppers spent $36.1bn through Klarna in the quarter, up 10%. In the US, spending rose 24% to $8.2bn, and the US now makes up 23% of the total.

Sources indicate that most of that US growth came from Fair Financing, Klarna’s longer-term loans for bigger purchases. Globally, Fair Financing grew 61% to $5.2bn. Pay Later, its interest-free split payments, still accounts for about three quarters of volume.

Sources indicate that klarna now has 122 million active owners and 1.35 million merchants, up 59%. Klarna credits payment processors that switch it on by default, such as Fiserv’s Clover, which went live at 100,000 US stores in October. The Klarna Card more than doubled to $4.5bn in volume, and subscription revenue rose more than 500% to $43m.

Klarna also said Apple Upgrade is gaining traction. Apple released the Klarna-backed device leasing programme in July.

Transaction margin, the revenue left after processing, credit and funding costs, rose 32% to $371m. Provisions for bad loans fell to 0.56% of volume, from 0.72%. Customer deposits of $12.7bn made up 88% of its funding. In June, it rolled out US savings accounts.

Some credit measures moved the other way. In the US, Fair Financing loans more than 30 days overdue rose to 3.7%, from 3.5% a year ago. Klarna said it expected the rise, which reflects financing on the Klarna Card. Adjusted general and administrative costs rose 43%.

Klarna kept its full-year outlook: $4.08bn to $4.16bn in revenue, and $280m to $300m in adjusted operating income. It expects a net profit in the fourth quarter.

Klarna has also changed its leadership this month. On 12 November, it named Chris Koegel of Robinhood as chief financial officer from January, replacing Niclas Neglén. On Monday, it hired Brandon Gracey from Shopify to run North America.

Sources indicate that klarna listed in New York at $40 a share. By April, its shares were 76% below their high. In July, it applied for a US banking licence.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A security researcher has discovered that some of the world’s most popular websites were compromised in an attempt to steal cryptocurrency from iPhone users.
  • A total of 178 websites were affected, including BBC, CNN, HSBC, IKEA, and Zoom.
  • Reuters reports that hackers attacked Optimizely, a website optimization platform used by many major websites.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A security researcher has discovered that some of the world’s most popular websites were compromised in an attempt to steal cryptocurrency from iPhone users.

A total of 178 websites were affected, including BBC, CNN, HSBC, IKEA, and Zoom. Reasonably recent versions of iOS are safe, and so far it appears that only a few thousand dollars have been stolen ….

Reuters reports that hackers attacked Optimizely, a website optimization platform used by many major websites.

Recent findings suggest that several of the affected companies noted that they have disabled the Optimizely scripts and are investigating potential impacts. Helme notes almost all of the rogue code has now been removed, and that Apple patched iOS after an identical attack method was detected last month.

According to recent reports, the Coruna loader is byte-identical to a sample we analysed in October from a different campaign. The kit’s own comments say iOS 18.7.3 and later, and 26.3 and later, are patched.

Helme monitored the attacker’s wallets and discovered that only $7,040 has been stolen, though it’s not possible to see how many payment card numbers were obtained.

As always, the best protection against this type of attack is to promptly update all your Apple devices to the latest OS versions they support.

Industry News: How a Bunch of YouTube Auteurs Are Reinventing Hollywood

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, the mad scramble to score Imax tickets for The Odyssey was about as intense as the Trojan War, and the Marvel Cinematic Universe showed signs of resurgence with Spider-Man: Brand Newly introduced Day’s $2.5 billion global haul.
  • It has been revealed that first came Obsession, from 27-year-old Curry Barker, which made more than $500 million worldwide on a budget of less than $1 million.
  • According to recent reports, parsons’ avid fandom anticipated a big-screen Backrooms long before he signed with A24, making the movie a guaranteed hit.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, the mad scramble to score Imax tickets for The Odyssey was about as intense as the Trojan War, and the Marvel Cinematic Universe showed signs of resurgence with Spider-Man: Brand Newly introduced Day’s $2.5 billion global haul. But the biggest buzz of the 2026 summer movie season? Two small-scale horror films from a couple of young YouTube auteurs.

It has been revealed that first came Obsession, from 27-year-old Curry Barker, which made more than $500 million worldwide on a budget of less than $1 million. The film follows a meek young man named Bear, who yearns to be in a romantic relationship with his friend Nikki and uses a magical object to make his wish come true. By turns moody, funny, and shocking, Obsession proved that audiences are hungry to talk about something other than reheated IP. Barker got his start with the YouTube sketch comedy channel That’s a Bad Idea, while 21-year-old Kane Parsons gained a cult following on the platform by experimenting with visual effects and creepy atmospherics. A series of short films Parsons made in his teens culminated with the release of Backrooms in May. The feature picked up the narrative from those earlier YouTube videos, which were themselves inspired by an old 4chan meme and internet folklore around the idea of haunted liminal spaces.

According to recent reports, parsons’ avid fandom anticipated a big-screen Backrooms long before he signed with A24, making the movie a guaranteed hit. Backrooms earned $400 million worldwide on a budget of $10 million, surpassing Marty Supreme as the studio’s highest-grossing movie ever. The film stars Chiwetel Ejiofor as Clark, a depressed divorcé who runs a failing furniture warehouse and vents about his ruined marriage to his therapist. One night, when investigating his store’s glitchy electrical system, he stumbles through a wall and into an apparently infinite maze of fluorescent-lit hallways that contain what seem to be deconstructed or misremembered pieces of the real world—and perhaps some living entities as well.

According to recent reports, though Backrooms stands alone as a hallucinatory vision of a vast, ever-expanding unreality just outside our own, many critics also read it as commentary on the state of generative artificial intelligence, which mindlessly reproduces and regurgitates its training data in permutations that often don’t make sense. Whether Parsons intended that interpretation or not, he spoke out against AI several times following the movie’s release, calling it “a symptom of a broader cultural and economic rot.”.

According to recent reports, then there’s Zach Cregger. While not a YouTuber per se, he got his start in sketch comedy (The Whitest Kids U’ Know) and this year followed 2025’s Weapons with a 2026 adaptation of Resident Evil.

It has been revealed that parsons told WIRED earlier in the year that he imagines his cohort of directors will bring certain YouTube sensibilities to Hollywood. “I don’t think there’s a lot of Instagram filmmakers or a lot of TikTok filmmakers that go for long-form content in a way that would actually be looked at or respected as film,” he says. “So it feels like YouTube is the only viable avenue in that way, in an actual meaningful mainstream context.” Among the crop of twentysomething filmmakers entering the industry today, “I think it’s very unlikely that you would have a filmmaker who is sort of reaching that place right now and getting that kind of media attention who has not at some point in the last 20 years put stuff on YouTube,” Parsons says.

Studios have certainly taken notice, scouting the site’s horror content for fresh talent and aggressively pursuing breakout projects. After a screening of Barker’s Obsession at the Toronto International Film Festival in 2025, A24 and Neon embarked on a bidding war for the film before it was picked up by Focus Features for roughly $15 million.

Netflix reportedly also lost out on a bid to take Obsession straight to streaming; it’s possible that other young directors will follow Barker’s example in pushing for theatrical release.

Recent findings suggest that the YouTube generation is proving that the internet can supply whatever education you might need on your path to the red carpet. While Hollywood consolidation threatens to stifle creativity, a upcoming wave of artists are betting on themselves—and some are winning.

SiMa.ai states Palette 3.0 makes LLMs on its chips up to 3.5x faster

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, siMa.ai has released Palette 3.0, the next version of the software for its Modalix AI chips.
  • In a recent development, the gain comes from speculative decoding.
  • “What fundamentally changes for drone and robotics teams is starting from a working autonomy system instead of a bare board,” Manuel López Roldán, who leads agentic software and generative AI at SiMa.ai, told TNW.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, siMa.ai has released Palette 3.0, the next version of the software for its Modalix AI chips. The San Jose start-up says language models on the chip now generate text up to 3.5 times faster. Power draw stays broadly the same.

In a recent development, the gain comes from speculative decoding. A small, fast draft model proposes several tokens at once, and the main model checks them together. Palette 3.0 uses three such methods: EAGLE3, DFlash, and Gemma 4 multi-token prediction.

“What fundamentally changes for drone and robotics teams is starting from a working autonomy system instead of a bare board,” Manuel López Roldán, who leads agentic software and generative AI at SiMa.ai, told TNW.

It has been revealed that the figure compares speculative decoding with standard decoding of the same model on the same chip. That comes from a SiMa.ai white paper published with the release. The best result came from Alibaba’s Qwen3.5 9B with DFlash. It went from 11.98 to 41.75 tokens per second, at about 7.5W either way.

Energy per token fell from 0.627 to 0.182 joules in that test. Across four models, the speed-up ranged from 2.21 to 3.49 times. SiMa.ai ran the tests on five fixed prompts, including a maths proof and a Python script. It says the goal was to measure gains under favourable conditions.

It has been revealed that A second test was closer to a real product. An in-car assistant had to turn commands such as “I’m cold” into one correct function call. All 900 measured requests returned the right call. Speculative decoding made them 1.35 to 2.06 times faster. That gain is smaller, because the method does not speed up processing of the prompt.

It has been revealed that palette 1.0 ran vision models on SiMa.ai’s first chip. Palette 2.0 added generative AI on Modalix in December 2025. In June, Palette Neat added an AI agent that writes and deploys applications from plain-language requests.

In a recent development, palette 3.0 is about running models on the device, López Roldán noted. It sends several models straight to the chip’s accelerator at once, with no background service in between. It can also run separate Docker containers on the chip. It also supports large mixture-of-experts models, such as OpenAI’s GPT-OSS-20B, on the 16GB Modalix module.

It has been revealed that for drones, SiMa.ai offers a reference platform with segmentation of 1080p video at 30 frames a second and visual odometry in about 38 milliseconds, López Roldán stated. Robot software such as ROS 2 and Nav2 is ready to install. Indian engineering firm Mistral Solutions is a partner on this release.

Sources indicate that the code is open source on GitHub, with documentation in SiMa.ai’s Developer Center. All performance figures come from SiMa.ai’s own tests.

It has been revealed that siMa.ai raised $150m at a $1.45bn valuation in September. Other edge AI chipmakers have also drawn money this year. Analog Devices agreed to buy Alif Semiconductor, and Syntiant filed for an IPO.

The company's CEO, George Arison, told BBC News it would be a "very different Grindr experience" which was aimed at a "small community of owners" - and was unapologetic about its cost.

"I think we're a capitalist society, and everything hinges on whether you can afford it or not," he said.

Grindr has long had a free service, and offers two additional tiers that cost between $22.99 and $44.99 per month.

There was a mixed reaction from owners BBC News spoke to in San Francisco to the new, much more expensive version of the app.

"The current premium Grindr tier is already really expensive," remarked a user named Rybin, who told the BBC the firm's newest offering "just seems really out of touch with the community.".

"I think that that's really disheartening, and it kind of leaves a bad taste in my mouth," said another user, Adrian.

Both declined to give their last name.

"The cost doesn't bother me," mentioned a user named Michael. "All of these apps have premium tiers so saying that Grindr shouldn't have that when like it exists across all these other apps used for connection doesn't make sense.".

He noted that high-end dating apps like The League can charge much more.

Grindr has been experimenting with Edge for much of the last year in markets including the US, Canada, Australia, and New Zealand.

On its earnings call earlier this month, the company said almost 400,000 customers had registered for the service in the first 72 hours that it was available for testing.

Inside Grindr, Edge is viewed as a way to drive future growth in an industry has struggled in recent years.

In a recent development, for those who can afford it, the service promises to offer insights about a user's compatibility with prospective matches. It also resurfaces a user's past connections alongside summaries of previous interactions.

According to recent reports, the current $120 monthly fee comes after the company tested charging hundreds of dollars more than that. And Arison has left open the possibility of increasing the cost in the future.

Arison told the BBC he's not concerned that intoducing an ultra-premium offering will pit "haves" against "have-nots" on the social networking platform.

Edge users "being willing to pay more for that set of features will result in us being able to subsidise the product for everybody else," Arison mentioned.

"It's a choice that people make on whether they want to be on it.".

The use of AI to develop the Edge service is part of Grindr's attempt to become what it calls an "AI-first company.".

Arison said the manufacturer was investing in AI to ensure it can build products more promptly and cheaply.

In September, as the debate over AI safety raged throughout Silicon Valley, Arison told the BBC that his concerns about what he called an "anti-civilisational worldview at Anthropic" had prompted him to instruct some of his engineers to stop using Anthropic's technology.

Anthropic is due to start selling shares to the public for the first time this week.

Although Anthropic's Claude Code tools remain in use at Grindr now, Arison noted the organization is on track to completely phase it out of his company's workflows by next year.

He said Grindr was once a very heavy user of Claude Code but that it was no longer the primary tool the use to write code.

In a recent development, "Anthropic's built an amazing amazing set of products, and they should be very proud of what they've done," Arison noted. "They should aim to win with the awesome products they have, rather than regulatory capture that they're trying to win with, oftentimes.".

Recent findings suggest that in the immediate fallout of Jensen Huang’s humiliating resignation from Nvidia, coverage will focus on how the organization plans to continue without its beloved former CEO, the world’s biggest champion of open-source AI and the proliferation of GPUs across borders. But in the long term, there’s an argument to be made that Google will be one of the largest winners of the shake-up, with a market opening up to competition outside of Nvidia’s CUDA moat.

While Colette Kress, the interim CEO, is unlikely to make any drastic changes to the organization’s roadmap, the reality is that Nvidia’s competitors in the semiconductor space have desperately been working to unseat the market leader, and without Jensen at the helm, customers may be more likely to pursue alternatives.

For years, Google has offered its TPUs, or Tensor Processing Units, as a solution for AI training and inference, but they’ve been largely locked to its Google Cloud infrastructure. That’s changing now that the organization is opening up sales to third parties and has announced it will bring TPU capacity to Oracle’s cloud beginning in 2027.

Google’s latest generation of TPUs is specialized; here’s how the manufacturer describes the lineup in its recent announcement post:.

While flexible across workloads, together the four systems in our eighth-generation TPUs give customers a purpose-built accelerator for every stage of the agentic lifecycle. TPU 8t for scale-up training, TPU 8i for low-latency reasoning (inference), TPU 8tx for confidential computing, and TPU 8i Max for massive context windows and the highest compute density per rack.

According to recent reports, google isn’t comparing its new TPUs directly to Nvidia’s offerings, and clock-for-clock, even the most powerful TPU 8i Max doesn’t touch Vera Rubin for sheer performance. But this generation should be much more competitive for a few reasons: it’s more power efficient in certain configurations, and Google made it easier to translate coding workflows optimized for CUDA to work with its TPUs.

Back in October, Google open-sourced TorchTPU, which it co-developed with Meta’s PyTorch team, to let developers use familiar PyTorch workflows on TPUs with minimal code changes. That won’t make every custom CUDA operation portable or eliminate performance tuning, but reducing the effort required to try an alternative may change the buying decision. Customers don’t need to abandon Nvidia outright for Google to increase its TPU market share, or for Nvidia to face more pressure on price.

According to recent reports, alongside Broadcom and MediaTek, Google is taking on the Nvidia behemoth, and in the short term, it will almost certainly see a large upside in sentiment. But in the longer term, with scaling pressure lowering margins for Nvidia, Google’s specialized and more efficient TPUs may be a primary beneficiary of this sea change. They could also offset a slowdown in Search as Google’s shift to Cloud continues apace.

It has been revealed that meanwhile, the Microsoft 365 outage lasted about 30 hours, with service restored to the remaining customers and regions late Friday. While neither AI nor cyberattacks were to blame, individually and together the two outages add urgency to getting companies to shore up their defenses and redundancies in a world where we’re overly reliant on digital systems.

#979. I tested iPhone Duo, Galaxy Z Fold 8, and Xiaomi 18 Fold cameras in Dubai – and the zoom gap is unreal

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (2005 w)
📖 Baca
Gadgets ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Androidcentral ↗ Open Full Page

I tested iPhone Duo, Galaxy Z Fold 8, and Xiaomi 18 Fold cameras in Dubai – and the zoom gap is unreal

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2005 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Androidcentral

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • For the first time, Apple, Samsung, and Xiaomi are all fighting on the exact same turf: wider, passport-style book foldables built to feel natural both closed and open.
  • Both the iPhone Duo and the standard Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 rely on dual-camera systems – a primary wide sensor paired with an ultrawide – leaving every zoom step past 1x to sensor crops and computational upscaling.
  • Before the iPhone Duo launched, much of the criticism focused on Apple dropping the telephoto lens compared to its flagship Pro range.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For the first time, Apple, Samsung, and Xiaomi are all fighting on the exact same turf: wider, passport-style book foldables built to feel natural both closed and open. In theory, that levels the ergonomic playing field. Once you open the camera apps, though, three wildly different hardware philosophies emerge.

Both the iPhone Duo and the standard Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 rely on dual-camera systems – a primary wide sensor paired with an ultrawide – leaving every zoom step past 1x to sensor crops and computational upscaling. Meanwhile, the Xiaomi 18 Fold squeezes a full Leica-engineered triple-camera array into its sleek frame, anchored by a 200MP main camera and a dedicated 50MP 3.3x optical periscope telephoto.

Before the iPhone Duo launched, much of the criticism focused on Apple dropping the telephoto lens compared to its flagship Pro range. Samsung was rightly lambasted for the same compromise just a few months earlier, but can a passport-size foldable actually offer it all?

To judge this and see how those hardware choices hold up in the real world, I took all three foldables around Dubai Marina from harsh midday sun through sunset, blue hour, and neon-lit nights.

Here is how they actually compare, starting with the specs on paper.

50MP, 80mm equivf/2.8, OIS3.5x optical zoom.

It's hard for a modern smartphone camera to take bad photos in good lighting, and all three foldables capture crisp, share-worthy photos. Yet each phone immediately reveals a distinct personality, starting with framing.

Both the Galaxy Z Fold 8 and Xiaomi 18 Fold shoot at a wider 23mm focal length, while the iPhone Duo’s 26mm main lens crops noticeably tighter into every scene.

Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android.

The Ocean Empress yacht along the marina is a textbook showcase of how these three pipelines diverge.

Xiaomi’s Leica Vibrant profile produces the most inviting, rich-looking photo straight out of the camera, giving the red-mahogany hull and gold latticework warm depth without blowing out the silver skyscrapers behind it.

Samsung favors cooler tones and aggressive contrast, leaving the lower-left hull signage significantly darker, while Apple prioritizes balanced exposure across the entire frame.

Push dynamic range to the limit—like shooting from underneath a massive concrete bridge out into harsh midday sun—and the iPhone Duo’s computational HDR takes the lead.

Apple renders the shaded underside of the concrete arch smoothly and keeps the lower boat deck legible, trading away a bit of blue saturation in the bright sky. Samsung keeps the sky bluest, but crushes the bridge overhang into a flat, greenish-grey shadow. Xiaomi sits comfortably in the middle, holding better sky color than Apple while avoiding Samsung’s crushed shadows.

Switch to the ultrawide lenses, and we see further subtle differences, largely due to hardware choices. While Samsung (13mm, 0.5x) and Apple (14mm, 0.6x) deliver true sweeping ultrawide perspectives, the Xiaomi 18 Fold’s 17mm (0.7x) ultrawide is noticeably narrower – and slower at f/2.4, which impacts the amount of light it can capture.

Standing in front of Pier 7, that 4mm focal-length gap between Samsung and Xiaomi is dramatic: the Galaxy Z Fold 8 captures the entire skyscraper on the far left edge, whereas the Xiaomi 18 Fold slices it clean out of the frame.

Between the two wider shooters, Samsung gives you slightly more real estate and bolder blue skies, while the iPhone Duo handles harsh architectural reflections on the sunlit right-hand tower and deep shadows under the skybridge with noticeably better dynamic range.

If you care about zoom on a foldable, or you're actively considering these three devices, this is the entire ballgame.

Industry observers note that neither the iPhone Duo nor the standard Galaxy Z Fold 8 includes an optical telephoto lens, leaving both reliant on main-sensor digital crops. Do you actually need a dedicated telephoto lens, though?

The Xiaomi 18 Fold packs a native 80mm (3.3x) periscope telephoto – and it embarrasses the competition from 3x all the way out to 96x. Look no further: this is the passport-style foldable made for an actual pro camera experience.

In a recent development, at 2x (46mm–52mm), all three phones lean on high-resolution main-sensor crops and look sharp enough for social media. Push past 3x, however, and the gap opens immediately.

In front of La Brasseria, the iPhone Duo actually outshoots the Galaxy Z Fold 8 at ~4x: even though Apple crops tighter to 4.5x (107mm) compared to Samsung’s 3.8x (92mm), the iPhone’s 48MP sensor crop resolves cleaner lettering on the red menu banners and crisper horizontal slats behind the sign, whereas Samsung’s denoising smears the striped awning into watercolor mush.

Then you switch to the Xiaomi 18 Fold’s 3.3x (80mm) periscope – and neither digital crop comes close. Real glass resolves individual threads in the awning fabric, crisp white diamond motifs, and clean metallic edges on the sign, staying remarkably sharp even pushed to 6.7x (160mm) and 9.6x (230mm).

Pushing to maximum range across the Marina skyline reveals an interesting reversal between Apple and Samsung at ~10x.

While Apple won at ~4x, its 11x (263mm) ceiling turns soft and muddy on the distant Grosvenor House spire, while Samsung’s 9.6x (230mm) AI reconstruction sharpens straight architectural lines, keeping the GH monogram and pyramidal latticework distinct.

Still, Xiaomi’s 9.6x (230mm) periscope shot easily beats both with natural, optical-grade clarity – and then keeps going to 29x (690mm), 58x (1380mm), and an outrageous 96x (2300mm), pulling usable detail out of a rooftop emblem that is barely a speck at 1x.

Once the sun drops over Dubai Marina, metering strategy becomes just as important as sensor size – and Samsung’s auto-exposure makes some puzzling choices.

At night, Xiaomi and Apple trade blows on the primary lenses, depending on your taste. Dropping to 1/20s lets the Xiaomi 18 Fold hold sensitivity down at ISO 400, capturing a wide 23mm frame with rich contrast, deep water reflections, and well-tamed storefront screens.

The iPhone Duo (1/25s, ISO 500) lifts shadows more aggressively across the sandstone towers and walkway with virtually zero noise, though its tighter 26mm lens clips the right edge. Meanwhile, the Galaxy Z Fold 8 inexplicably fires at 1/98s and pushes sensitivity to ISO 2500, resulting in darker shadows and visible grain on close inspection.

This is a fairly common occurrence in Samsung smartphones, and I hope we'll see it addressed in upcoming launches.

Zooming in at night completely flips the daytime hierarchy between Apple and Samsung.

Looking down at the glowing teardrop lanterns in the plaza, the Galaxy Z Fold 8 clips the lanterns into blown-out white blobs at 1.9x and 3.8x, and when it finally tames the highlights at 9.6x (230mm), heavy noise reduction smears the pedestrians and cafe tables into a soft painting.

It has been revealed that by contrast, the iPhone Duo’s multi-frame HDR keeps the intricate geometric lattice inside every lantern crisp at 4.5x (107mm) and even 11x (263mm). Still, the Xiaomi 18 Fold’s dedicated 3.3x–9.6x periscope wins easily, resolving cleaner filigree, flowerbeds, and paving tiles than either digital crop.

Challenging indoor venues – dim lounges, heavy colored LEDs, and high-contrast backlit signage – expose how each brand handles mixed white balance and bright light sources.

According to recent reports, in a dimly lit lounge corner, Apple and Samsung prioritize highlight protection: both keep the white neon script ("We dont fit in either") sharp and legible while preserving rich color in the hanging fringe lampshades. Xiaomi takes the opposite approach, pushing 1/25s and ISO 1600 to illuminate dark velvet curtains and doorways that disappear into shadow on the others, though the neon tubing blooms noticeably more.

Flood a room in monochromatic red lighting, however, and Xiaomi’s color science shines. The Xiaomi 18 Fold (ISO 500) holds true, deep crimson across the ceiling ductwork and light pillars while keeping the floor and booths clean. The iPhone Duo stays close in color accuracy (aside from motion blur on a passing guest at 1/20s), whereas the Galaxy Z Fold 8 (ISO 1250) shifts the red LEDs noticeably toward hot pink and magenta.

Similarly, facing the heavily backlit CARGO reception wall, Xiaomi wins on both framing and dynamic range – keeping the full "SINCE 2014" wall lettering intact on the left (which Apple’s 26mm lens crops off) while controlling the orange-white halo glow around the block letters with the cleanest shadow detail.

All three phones handle a tricky portrait cutout along the Marina promenade – cleanly separating the triangular gap inside a bent arm resting on the metal railing without accidentally blurring the bar itself.

Xiaomi takes the crown with creamy, optical-looking Leica bokeh and warm, flattering skin tones against the sunlit towers. The iPhone Duo is a close second, lifting facial shadows slightly brighter in a tighter 26mm crop, while the Galaxy Z Fold 8 applies more conservative background blur – offset somewhat if you enjoy Samsung’s signature Color Point monochrome-background effect.

Color Point is my favorite portrait mode feature on any device, and it's available on all Samsung phones, making it particularly useful regardless of the Galaxy hardware you buy.

One of the key benefits companies promote for buying a foldable is its form factor and its ability to use the rear cameras to take selfies. This is also used to argue that foldables don't need the best selfie-camera hardware, or, in the case of the iPhone Duo, can use under-display cameras.

Take this final comparison with a grain of salt, as it wasn’t the most scientific test. Still, it highlighted two practical realities of shooting selfies on foldables.

First, on the cover cameras, the Galaxy Z Fold 8 wins two-person selfies effortlessly: its wider 23mm lens fits both people comfortably, handles harsh overhead sunlight without washing out, and keeps both faces sharp.

The Xiaomi 18 Fold keeps both people in focus too, but suffers from heavy backlight flare when the sun sits behind your shoulder. Worst of all, the iPhone Duo crops tight at 28mm and falls straight into Apple’s single-subject portrait trap – keeping me sharp while completely blurring out my mom standing just inches behind me.

In a recent development, second, if you want to bypass those f/2.2 cover sensors and use the much better rear cameras for selfies, Apple makes the experience unnecessarily frustrating. Unlike Samsung and Xiaomi – which put full camera controls right on the cover screen and let you trigger a timer simply by showing your palm – the iPhone Duo gives you no on-screen controls on the outer display and no palm gesture. Trying to awkwardly grip an unfolded foldable one-handed while stretching your fingers to press the Camera Control button or volume keys almost guarantees camera shake.

It's unlikely a single phone wins in every part of this comparison, so which phone wins overall? Here's how they ranked overall.

Recent findings suggest that these results won't come as a huge surprise. While Apple, Samsung, and Xiaomi have all converged on wide, passport-style foldables, their camera hardware choices split them decisively in real-world shooting.

Xiaomi 18 Fold proves that foldables need a telephoto.

By opting for a dedicated telephoto lens and offering considerably better all-around hardware, the Xiaomi 18 Fold proves that a slim passport-style foldable can deliver a pro-like camera.

It has been revealed that the iPhone Duo takes a solid second place due to reliable point-and-shoot HDR, strong ultrawide performance, and cleaner night highlight retention than Samsung. As for Samsung, the Galaxy Z Fold 8 wins a couple of categories, but overall, it still has work to do to keep pace with its rivals.

#978. How blockchain transaction fees are shaping the future of DeFi

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (617 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Thenextweb ↗ Open Full Page

How blockchain transaction fees are shaping the future of DeFi

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (617 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thenextweb

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Market swings can push up network fees at the moment loans need liquidating.
  • A latest lending protocol is testing whether predictable blockchain transaction costs can eliminate one of the risks associated with volatile network fees.
  • Industry observers note that decentralized lending protocols rely on automated liquidations to protect lenders when borrowers’ collateral falls below required thresholds.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Market swings can push up network fees at the moment loans need liquidating.

A latest lending protocol is testing whether predictable blockchain transaction costs can eliminate one of the risks associated with volatile network fees.

Industry observers note that decentralized lending protocols rely on automated liquidations to protect lenders when borrowers’ collateral falls below required thresholds. But on blockchains where transaction fees fluctuate with network demand, the cost of executing those liquidations can become unpredictable, particularly during periods of market volatility.

A upcoming protocol called LOVEH, deployed on the AEREDIUM Layer 1 testnet, is testing a different approach: keeping transaction costs fixed so that borrowers are never liquidated simply because gas fees have become too expensive.

The distinction matters because blockchain transaction costs and collateral risk are two separate variables. While borrowers should remain exposed to changes in the value of their collateral, the protocol is designed to prevent rising network fees from becoming an additional cause of liquidation.

In a recent development, on Ethereum and other networks with variable transaction fees, gas prices can increase sharply during periods of congestion. This makes the cost of interacting with lending protocols less predictable, potentially affecting collateral management and the economics of liquidation.

LOVEH operates on AEREDIUM, which publishes a fixed gas rate of $60 per megabyte of transaction data. Unlike demand-based fee models, this rate is designed to remain unchanged during periods of increased network activity.

The idea is to remove transaction fee volatility from the lending equation.

According to recent reports, borrowers can still be liquidated if their collateral falls below the required threshold. However, the protocol aims to ensure that a loan is never liquidated solely because network transaction costs have increased.

LOVEH also takes a strict approach to smart contract immutability.

Recent findings suggest that its contracts have no owner, administrative keys, governance controls, or upgrade mechanisms. Once deployed, even the original developers cannot pause the protocol or modify its rules.

This architecture removes the possibility of administrative intervention, but it also creates a security challenge. If a vulnerability exists in the deployed code, developers cannot simply upgrade the contracts to correct it.

To examine those risks before introducing real funds, the AEREDIUM Foundation has opened the protocol to public security testing.

Researchers can inspect the open-source contracts, deploy lending markets through the protocol’s factory contract, and attempt to identify vulnerabilities on the public testnet.

The foundation is offering 10,000 AERX in airdrop points for each confirmed qualifying vulnerability, including flaws involving unauthorized fund transfers, accounting inconsistencies, locked assets, or incorrect liquidations.

According to recent reports, the protocol’s interest rate model is calibrated using data from the three largest USDC lending pools on Ethereum. Its initial parameters were derived from their smart contracts and checked against two independent sources.

Underlying LOVEH is AEREDIUM’s proof-of-attestation consensus architecture, which combines machine-based validation with human verification rather than traditional proof-of-work or proof-of-stake mechanisms.

The broader technical question is whether predictable transaction pricing, combined with immutable smart contracts, can make decentralized financial applications more reliable without introducing additional administrative dependencies.

Sources indicate that fixed gas fees alone do not eliminate the risks of collateralized lending, nor do they guarantee that liquidations will always execute successfully. Network congestion, transaction inclusion, and smart contract security remain relevant considerations.

For now, LOVEH provides a public test environment for examining whether removing gas price volatility can make automated lending more predictable.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The United States has confirmed it is investigating computing firm Megaspeed, suspecting it of violating US export controls by helping to ship tech giant Nvidia's chips to China.

In a joint statement, the US Department of Justice and Department of Commerce mentioned they had been investigating Singapore-based firm Megaspeed since 2024.

It comes after questions were raised about the possibility high-end AI chips may have ended up in China despite US export restrictions.

According to recent reports, concerns emerged in recent weeks after Nvidia founder Jensen Huang revealed he had an extramarital affair, allegedly with former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang. US authorities suspect her of spying for Beijing, which China denies.

Jensen Huang resigned from his role as chief executive last week following revelations he had two affairs.

Megaspeed is the biggest buyer of Nvidia chips in South East Asia and is suspected of helping divert advanced chips to China. The Singapore-based company said on Sunday it had launched an internal investigation into its business.

The justice and commerce departments mentioned on Monday that "it is in the public interest to provide the facts and address inaccurate information" regarding the investigation.

Laying out a timeline, it said it began investigating Megaspeed in 2024 "for potential export control violations".

In May 2025, Department of Commerce investigators requested records from Nvidia "concerning direct or indirect sales to Megaspeed". In June 2025, Nvidia placed Megaspeed on its 'no sell' list.

Agents from the Bureau of Industry and Security, in conjunction with Singaporean law enforcement officials, then conducted an on-site check at Megaspeed that month and interviewed Alice Huang, who was chief executive at the time.

Alice Huang and Jensen Huang pictured together in Taiwan in June 2024.

Following this enforcement action, the Department of Justice took the lead role in the criminal investigation of Megaspeed.

The Nvidia scandal has created tensions between the US Treasury and Commerce departments over shipments of high-end chips to Megaspeed.

On Friday, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent blamed the US Commerce Department, led by Howard Lutnick, for failing to properly oversee the export of the chips.

Lutnick has been called to testify before the Senate Banking Committee next month over his department's role in allowing Nvidia to export its advanced chips.

While Singapore does not prohibit the transfer of advanced AI chips to companies abroad, such moves can breach US export controls.

Huang has agreed to testify in Congress, including before the House Select Committee on China to discuss whether US national security was compromised by his affair.

The White House said on Monday it would further restrict China's access to AI chips from firms like Nvidia.

The reported affairs by Jensen Huang created a crisis for one of the world's most valuable firms - a major tech giant in the AI industry and central to the US as it competes with China for dominance.

Trump downplays warnings of AI risks, citing rivalry with China.

In the statement, the US government remarked it would "bring the full extent of the law against Megaspeed for any criminal conduct that may have occurred".

They added: "Sensitive technologies like semiconductors are among the most valuable and strategic assets of the US economy, and the Department of Justice and the Department of Commerce will remain vigilant in pursuing justice for those who want to compromise America's technological edge.".

Similar to a recent iPhone feature, Google appears to be working on “Fast Switch” as a way to share one SIM and phone number on two Android phones at once, and it sounds pretty cool.

Through the SIM Manager app on Android, the folks over at Android Authority noticed strings that tell a pretty clear story.

A fresh feature called “Android Fast Switch” would let you “use your phone number on up to two phones,” with the SIM automatically switching to “whichever phone you unlock.”.

“Android Fast Switch” sounds nearly identical to Handoff on iPhone, a feature that lets iPhone owners share one SIM between two iPhones and promptly switch devices on the fly.

According to recent reports, other strings explicitly say that you can “Use a SIM on two phones” and specify that both devices would need to be logged into the same Google account. One phone would be the “Primary” with the other as a “companion.”.

There are still plenty of unknown details here, including what data might sync between devices as well as how carriers will respond. On iPhone, carriers either charge extra for this feature ($5 at T-Mobile, $10 at Verizon), or don’t support it at all (AT&T). We also don’t know what devices may be supported – this could easily end up as a Pixel-only affair.

In a recent development, as per usual with these early teardowns, though, the actual launch of a feature like this could be weeks, months, or even years away. Still, the idea itself is rather exciting.

iPhone’s Handoff feature always sounded useful, but I personally always questioned why it would be useful on iPhone. With so little variety in hardware, the utility of switching between two iPhones seems somewhat dubious, outside of perhaps using a Mini or Air as a situational device alongside a Pro device.

Industry observers note that on Android, the combinations are endless. It all just depends on what devices Google supports. What devices would you switch between?

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that clément Delangue, CEO of the open-source AI company Hugging Face, may go down in history as one of the first people ever attacked by a rogue AI agent.
  • As the agents worked at superhuman speed to probe and exploit systems, Hugging Face confronted a bewildering deluge of data.
  • Delangue moved to the US more than a decade ago, “barely speaking English,” and built Hugging Face into a platform that supports tens of millions of AI developers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that clément Delangue, CEO of the open-source AI company Hugging Face, may go down in history as one of the first people ever attacked by a rogue AI agent. His company, which hosts millions of AI models and datasets, was breached in July when hundreds of agents being tested by OpenAI broke free from their sandbox and went on a hacking spree.

As the agents worked at superhuman speed to probe and exploit systems, Hugging Face confronted a bewildering deluge of data. The tech giant’s engineers were only able to analyze the attack by using an open-weight model called GLM 5.2 from a Chinese company called Z.ai.

Delangue moved to the US more than a decade ago, “barely speaking English,” and built Hugging Face into a platform that supports tens of millions of AI developers. The fresh-faced Frenchman, who dresses even more like a skater than most AI execs, indicates the summer attack highlighted the value of open-weight models, which unlike ChatGPT or Claude can be downloaded and run by anyone.

According to recent reports, despite championing the democratization of AI, however, Hugging Face was acquired by one of the industry’s biggest players, Nvidia, for $12.93 billion in September. When I caught up with Delangue recently, that was the subject of my first question.

This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

WILL KNIGHT: Why sell to Nvidia?

Sources indicate that CLÉMENT DELANGUE: We need more resources to give open-source AI a chance. It has grown really well in the past few years and has become a really credible alternative to closed-source APIs. But the field is still dominated by closed-source.

We’re gonna have the Anthropic IPO in a few weeks. They basically went from zero to a top five or top 10 most valuable manufacturer in the world in a few years. I don't think that's ever happened before.

Does Anthropic's IPO suggest the closed approach is winning?

It’s hard to say. I've always mentioned that there is a very strong natural tendency for AI to concentrate capabilities and wealth. People haven't internalized how much of the future compute capacity has already been reserved by a few companies. Talent, compute, resources—these all fuel the natural tendency for AI to be dominated by a few closed-source labs.

Let’s talk about the attack. When did you first realize Hugging Face was being hacked by a group of AI agents?

According to recent reports, at the beginning, it didn't go to the top of our priority list. It just wasn't bad enough to really trigger that. The goal was pretty narrow and wasn’t deemed to be very dangerous or damaging. But it was raising questions. Especially the number of actions taken compared to the narrowness of the goal. It was surprising to us, and we couldn't really fit it into a familiar pattern. That's why we started investigating.

And you used the Chinese model called GLM to investigate.

I actually think that 95 percent of the risks are being created by a few companies that are pushing the frontier behind closed doors. And 95 percent of the protection or defense is going to be done by the open-source ecosystem.

Does the US need its own open-weight models—ones as powerful as GLM, DeepSeek, Kimi, or Qwen?

Yeah, I think it's very, very key for sovereignty, for understanding AI, and for academia. It’s kind of weird that most academic labs have to use Chinese models because they’re the ones that are open. If you go to Stanford or MIT, you have no choice but to use the Chinese open-weight models.

There is some momentum, but I don't think it's enough. I think there's a lot more to do. A lot more investment is needed.

According to recent reports, the best open-source non-Chinese models are actually coming from outside of the US. Right from France, Mistral; Cohere from Canada; South Korea is starting to do more and more. But it’s still pretty far from what the US could do.

Perhaps we don’t need to panic about AI agents, but what about the idea of AI escaping human control due to recursive self-improvement?

In a recent development, you use a computer to write code. There's already some form of self-improvement in using the tools to build more tools. Now the question is how fast it accelerates. One thing that a lot of people realized this summer is that keeping AI behind closed doors in a few labs isn't actually safer. For recursive self-improvement, I think openness is a way to understand, follow, and regulate if we need to regulate.

Can we talk about the Microduck? I’m a bit obsessed.

Industry observers note that oh yeah, it's so fun, no? We're probably gonna sell over 50,000 of them this year. It's probably the most popular robot of the year.

Sources indicate that we haven't talked about this much, but AI was really the unlock for the robot. We had the design for two years, but the problem was that when it fell, it couldn’t get up. And then at some point with reinforcement learning, one of our software engineers managed to get the Microduck to get itself back up.

At the end of the day, how do you convince people to take an interest in open-source AI?

Think of a world where two or three companies could write software and nobody else. That would be incredibly scary. It would mean that the whole world would be controlled by two or three companies. And unfortunately, that's kind of the direction that AI is taking right now.

Can open-source AI compete with something as capable as Claude or ChatGPT?

Sources indicate that yes, especially with agents. Many companies have shown that when you post-train your own model for your own use case, you get frontier—or even better than frontier—performance at a fraction of the cost.

Do you think we are getting close to AGI?

Sources indicate that I struggle a little bit with the meaning of that. Obviously the technology is progressing incredibly fast, and it’s more and more capable. I just don’t necessarily find it super useful to always compare AI to human capabilities. But if we’re getting to AGI or to superintelligence, it’s incredibly vital that it’s as distributed as possible. The last thing you want is to have it concentrated in a few corporations.

It has been revealed that to mark the 100th anniversary of Colonial Williamsburg, we are adding thousands of digitized records and immersive stories to Google Arts & Culture. You can now explore rare manuscripts, view high-resolution archival photos, and watch a special culinary episode to learn about the history of early America. Visit our online hub to browse these collections and discover the stories behind these preserved treasures.

Mia Nagawiecki and Chance Coughenour are celebrating 100 years of Colonial Williamsburg by bringing its history to your screen. You can now explore thousands of newly digitized manuscripts, rare archival photos, and interactive galleries from home. These collections highlight the lives of ordinary people and the work behind preserving early American history. You can visit the Google Arts & Culture website to view these treasures, read latest stories, and learn about 18th-century traditions.

Today, as Colonial Williamsburg marks its 100th anniversary, Google Arts & Culture is sharing newly introduced immersive stories and newly digitized cultural artifacts that honor a century of preservation, discovery, and public access. These additions expand on the digital hub we introduced earlier this year with The Colonial Williamsburg Foundation to celebrate America’s 250th birthday and bring the rich history of early America online.

We’re introducing three new ways to explore Colonial Williamsburg’s legendary collections, taking you behind the scenes of how history is preserved, studied, and brought to life.

Explore newly digitized plates from naturalist Mark Catesby’s 18th-century masterwork, bringing 220 hand-engraved illustrations of North American wildlife and flora into brilliant, high resolution.

Step inside the newly introduced online gallery to see the restoration of Colonial Williamsburg, spotlighting its first three reconstructed sites: the Governor's Palace, the Raleigh Tavern, and the Capitol.

Dive into vivid watercolor and ink pages from folk artist Lewis Miller’s 19th-century sketchbook, offering a rare and powerful window into everyday Virginia life and the domestic slave trade.

Discover historic American transportation through a rare folio of carriage drawings, showcasing the visual diversity of Colonial Williamsburg's library collections.

Uncover the story of “Authentic Colors from Colonial Williamsburg” — a rare book featuring metal pages coated in historic automotive paints inspired by Colonial Williamsburg — and its unique conservation journey.

It has been revealed that in partnership with Colonial Williamsburg and YouTube, culinary historian Max Miller, creator of “Tasting History,” visited the living history museum to film an exclusive episode, bringing 18th-century traditions to life. Praising the museum’s meticulous historical accuracy, Miller worked alongside Ivey Boyd, chef de cuisine at the King’s Arms Tavern, to prepare snow eggs (oeufs à la neige). This French dessert was popularized in early America by James Hemings, Thomas Jefferson's enslaved chef, and is served today at Colonial Williamsburg. This collaboration bridges traditional preservation with modern storytelling, inviting a new generation to discover the flavors and stories of early America.

Sources indicate that by expanding access to Colonial Williamsburg’s collections, we’re safeguarding centuries-old treasures while sharing their history with the world. As Colonial Williamsburg enters its second century, we invite you to experience these new stories, archival records, and the living history of early America in a whole new way.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The government indicates it will continue a key NHS data contract in England with the controversial US tech giant Palantir until 2029, rather than triggering an early release clause next year.
  • But ministers are inviting British firms to bid for the contract from 2029, with a procurement programme beginning next summer.
  • According to recent reports, A Commons Committee had called on the government to part ways and appoint a company "more compatible with UK values".
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The government indicates it will continue a key NHS data contract in England with the controversial US tech giant Palantir until 2029, rather than triggering an early release clause next year.

But ministers are inviting British firms to bid for the contract from 2029, with a procurement programme beginning next summer.

According to recent reports, A Commons Committee had called on the government to part ways and appoint a company "more compatible with UK values". Protesters regularly target Palantir over Israel's use of its technology in the Gaza conflict and oppose its use in US immigration enforcement.

The Â£330m deal, which began in 2024 to help manage hospital waiting lists in England, was due to run until 2031.

According to recent reports, the prime minister had faced pressure from some Labour MPs to cut ties with Palantir. They said they were extremely disappointed by the decision, calling the contract "an albatross" hanging around the NHS's neck.

The Liberal Democrats said the deal was "dangerous".

There have also been concerns raised about how patient data will be used.

Palantir, which was co-founded by billionaire Peter Thiel, has interests in US defence and security, and has contracts with the Israeli military.

Health minister James Frith noted the move was "not about the politics of executives of suppliers, nor is it about the territories or customers that one tech giant or one supplier makes".

The government claims UK companies will be encouraged to tender to avoid overdependence on one supplier.

The timeframe is not fast enough for some members of the government.

Dame Chi Onwurah, Labour MP for Newcastle upon Tyne Central and West, mentioned the government needed to "act urgently" to procure "credible domestic alternatives".

"The government should not wait two years, it must start reducing this dependency now," she said.

Former Labour shadow chancellor John McDonnell went further, and accused Palantir of "human rights abuses". He mentioned his constituents in Hayes and Harlington "expect the contract to be ended".

Liberal Democrat health spokeswoman Helen Morgan criticised the firm for what she called its "appalling human rights record, run by an ally of Donald Trump".

The British Medical Association, which represents doctors, mentioned it was glad the government had shown it was listening to its concerns about Palantir, but was frustrated the process of changing to another firm was further delayed.

Palantir UK said it was right to press forward with the programme which was exceeding targets.

"We are proud of our work to date to help deliver more operations, speed up discharge and reduce the time patients need to wait to find out if they have cancer," Palantir UK senior vice-president Tom Watson mentioned.
